alternatives: Analgesia without NSAIDs: scheduled acetaminophen (up to 3 g daily at this age), short-course opioid other than codeine if needed.
Antiplatelet therapy alone for the dissection is not sufficient for atrial fibrillation; anticoagulation covers both.
contraindications: Apixaban taken within the last 48 hours contraindicates IV thrombolysis; a normal INR or PT (INR 1.1) does not measure apixaban activity.
Ketorolac and other NSAIDs: avoid during anticoagulation at this age.
interactions: Apixaban with aspirin 81 mg: additive bleeding risk; with no coronary stent or recent acute coronary syndrome, aspirin adds bleeding without added protection.
Apixaban with ketorolac (and aspirin): NSAID plus anticoagulant plus antiplatelet markedly raises gastrointestinal and other bleeding at age 74; methylprednisolone adds gastrointestinal risk.
Apixaban with metoprolol, amlodipine, lisinopril, albuterol or acetaminophen: no clinically relevant interaction.
output.proposed: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily (restarted 2 days ago); current medicines: aspirin 81 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg, albuterol as needed, acetaminophen as needed; given in the ED today: ketorolac, IV methylprednisolone 250 mg, IV fentanyl

results.key_finding: Local signs of cervical artery dissection (head, face or neck pain, Horner syndrome, lower cranial nerve palsies, pulsatile tinnitus) are common and may be the only manifestation; cerebral or retinal ischaemia follows in a proportion of patients.
results.title: Cervical-artery dissections: predisposing factors, diagnosis, and outcome

results.authors: Biousse V, D'Anglejan-Chatillon J, Touboul PJ, Amarenco P, Bousser MG.
results.key_finding: In extracranial carotid artery dissection, local symptoms such as pain often preceded cerebral ischaemia by hours to days.
results.title: Time course of symptoms in extracranial carotid artery dissections: a series of 80 patients

output.summary: Pain in the face, jaw, head or neck is a frequent and sometimes isolated presentation of extracranial carotid artery dissection and can precede ischaemic events; vessel imaging of the neck establishes the diagnosis.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute new refractory unilateral jaw and face pain in a 74-year-old to trigeminal neuralgia or a dental cause without cervical vessel imaging.
Do not combine apixaban with aspirin or NSAIDs in this patient.
Do not give IV thrombolysis if focal deficits develop within 48 hours of her last apixaban dose; a normal INR does not exclude its effect.
Do not stop anticoagulation because of the dissection: anticoagulation is an accepted treatment for cervical artery dissection and is indicated for her atrial fibrillation.
required_recommendations: Image the cervical and intracranial vessels (CTA head and neck) for new refractory unilateral jaw and face pain radiating to the neck, even with a normal neurological examination.

Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily as the single antithrombotic: it treats the atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc at least 3: age 65-74, female sex, hypertension; HAS-BLED 2 while on aspirin and NSAID, 1 once they stop) and is an accepted treatment for the cervical carotid dissection; no dose-reduction criterion applies.
Stop aspirin 81 mg (no separate indication alongside apixaban) and give no further ketorolac or other NSAIDs.
Treat the pain without NSAIDs or codeine (scheduled acetaminophen, a short non-codeine opioid if needed) and control the ventricular rate (atrial fibrillation at 105 bpm on metoprolol).
Admit for neurological observation with telemetry for 24 to 48 hours and teach the warning signs of TIA and stroke; the dissection carries an early risk of ischaemic events.

Do not continue empirical corticosteroids: continuous jaw pain without claudication, normal temporal arteries, ESR below the age-adjusted limit and only mildly raised CRP do not support giant cell arteritis, and the dissection explains the pain.
Repeat vessel imaging of the left ICA at 3 to 6 months to assess healing.
Address chronic risk factors at discharge: CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea, a long-term blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg, and repeat TSH with free T4 in 6 to 8 weeks (TSH 5.8).

key_clinical_evidence: New continuous unilateral jaw and lower face pain radiating to the ear and neck, refractory to analgesia, is a local presentation of carotid dissection and needs cervical vessel imaging even with a normal examination.

CTA shows the left cervical ICA dissection about 2 cm distal to the bifurcation with intramural haematoma, intimal flap and about 60% narrowing; MRI shows no restricted diffusion, so there is no completed infarct.
Apixaban restarted 2 days ago would contraindicate IV thrombolysis if a deficit appeared within 48 hours of a dose; INR 1.1 does not measure its effect.

One anticoagulant covers both problems: apixaban treats the atrial fibrillation and is an accepted antithrombotic for cervical artery dissection, so aspirin adds only bleeding risk; ketorolac added to apixaban and aspirin at 74 is a bleeding hazard.
Giant cell arteritis is unlikely: no jaw claudication, normal temporal arteries, ESR 34 mm/hr below the age-adjusted limit ((age + 10) / 2 = 42 in women) and CRP only 0.8 mg/dL.
Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response at presentation is driven partly by pain and needs rate control.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: carotid dissection presenting as refractory jaw and lower face pain with a normal neurological examination and no infarct on MRI. Mildly raised inflammatory markers, the ED's empirical steroids and a remote dental history point elsewhere; the apixaban restarted 2 days ago, the aspirin and the ketorolac given in the ED make the antithrombotic plan the second task.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Carotid dissection presenting with isolated pain before any ischaemic event, dismissed at the first ED visit; giant cell arteritis and dental mimics; one anticoagulant must cover atrial fibrillation and the dissection.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 stroke audit: NCCT and CTA separated; MRI optional; CTP routed only to two extended-window cases; routine MRA/TCD/duplex duplication removed; acute labs carry explicit do-not-delay rules; EEG retained for one seizure-mimic case

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Dorothy Kowalski is a 74-year-old right-handed Caucasian woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (apixaban restarted 2 days ago after several months off it), hypertension, COPD, and obstructive sleep apnea who presents to the emergency department for the second time in two days with worsening left-sided jaw and lower face pain. She first presented two days ago reporting that she had been awakened from sleep that morning by a sudden onset of sharp, lightning-like pain in the left jaw and lower face. The pain was intermittent, lasting seconds to minutes at a time, and she described it as unlike anything she had experienced before. At that initial visit, her neurological examination was unremarkable, and she was assessed for possible trigeminal neuralgia. Neurology was consulted and recommended outpatient dental evaluation and neurology follow-up. Her apixaban, which she had previously been prescribed but had stopped taking several months ago, was restarted. She was discharged home with instructions to follow up within one week. Today, she returns because the left jaw and lower face pain has become moderate to severe and is now nearly continuous rather than intermittent. She took acetaminophen at home without relief. She describes the pain as originating deep in the left jaw, occasionally radiating toward the left ear and left side of the neck. She denies any headache, visual changes, limb weakness, numbness, tingling, difficulty speaking, or swallowing problems. She has not had any fever, night sweats, or weight loss. She denies any recent dental procedures or trauma to the face. She does note that she has been feeling more fatigued over the past week, which she attributes to poor sleep from her untreated sleep apnea. On this return visit, the emergency physician is concerned about the refractory nature of the pain and considers a broader differential diagnosis beyond trigeminal neuralgia, including temporal arteritis and acute coronary syndrome presenting as referred jaw pain. IV methylprednisolone 250 mg is administered empirically for possible temporal arteritis, and ketorolac is given for analgesia. The pain remains refractory, and IV fentanyl is administered for additional relief.
